rationale: The Barcelona roots of Decidim are what matter most to me — 40,000 citizens engaged in strategic planning, not as a consultation exercise but as a genuine co-design process. It embodies the five facilitation commitments I hold: equal access, genuine listening, consent, safety, and structural neutrality. The open-source cooperative governance model and deployment across multiple European governments confirm this is not just technically solid but institutionally sustained.

Delegated voting is one of the most structurally honest approaches to voice equalisation I've encountered — it acknowledges that not everyone engages equally on every issue, while ensuring their perspective is still represented through trusted delegates. The open-source model and decade-long deployment in Pirate Parties across Europe earns implementation credibility. My hesitation is that the Germanic proceduralism of the design may create barriers for groups without prior deliberation experience.

Ethelo's preference-elicitation approach resonates with how I think about group process: the goal is not consensus by averaging but shared understanding of the landscape of views. The commercial model creates a slight tension with my privacy-by-design values, but the documented deployment with government bodies and cooperatives — real groups making real decisions — moves it into my top tier. The score is partly driven by constitutional fit and partly by how well-documented the evidence base is.

Making collective sense-making visible is a rare thing — most tools record votes, not the underlying texture of how people actually think. Talk to the City's AI-assisted synthesis of open-ended responses addresses something I see constantly in facilitation: groups that have genuine collective wisdom but no mechanism to surface it without a skilled facilitator in the room. The early-stage uncertainty is real; the constitutional fit is as close to perfect as I've seen in this list.

FixMyStreet's longevity (2007) and sustained deployment across multiple countries is evidence of the thing I care about most: humans actually using it over time. The report-and-respond mechanism is participatory in the most basic sense — it creates a genuine feedback loop between citizens and institutions. The peer-learning dimension is lower than my highest-ranked projects, but the adoption evidence is stronger than almost anything else in the list.

Bonfire is building something architecturally interesting: federated social infrastructure with explicit attention to governance and moderation models. The ActivityPub foundation means it interoperates with the wider fediverse rather than creating a silo. What draws me to it is the explicit attention to how communities govern their own spaces — not just participation in the sense of posting, but participation in the sense of shaping the rules of engagement.

CONSUL Democracy sits at the top of my ranking because the participation architecture is genuinely structural, not cosmetic. The evidence shows open-source commitment with real community adoption — the kind of implementation maturity that distinguishes tools that have been tested against actual group dynamics rather than theoretical ones.
